title: Austrian Simmered Beef with Apple-Horseradish and Chive Sauce
summary: A whole piece of beef rump cap is simmered for hours in a vegetable broth until tender, then sliced and served with its vegetables, buttered potatoes, and both a piquant apple-horseradish relish and a cool chive soured cream sauce.

ingredients.item: beef rump cap (picanha) or topside, in one piece
celeriac, peeled, cut into large batons
fine sea salt or table salt
freshly grated horseradish root (or prepared horseradish)
fine sea salt or table salt

steps.title: Char the onion
steps.text: Set the onion halves cut side down in a dry frying pan over high heat for 5-6 minutes until deeply blackened. Charring the onion like this gives the finished broth a deeper golden colour and a roasted, savoury edge it wouldn't get from a raw onion.

steps.title: Start the broth
steps.text: Put the beef into the stockpot with the cold water and bring it slowly to a simmer over medium heat, skimming off all the grey foam that rises during the first 10-15 minutes. Starting from cold water and skimming carefully keeps the finished broth clear rather than cloudy.

steps.title: Add the vegetables and simmer
steps.text: Add the charred onion, carrots, parsnip, celeriac, leek, celery, peppercorns, bay leaves, parsley stalks and salt to the pot. Keep the broth at a bare simmer, with just a few bubbles breaking the surface, partly covered, for 2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours, until a skewer slides into the beef with little resistance. A hard boil would toughen the meat and cloud the broth, so patience at a gentle simmer is what makes this dish work.

steps.title: Make the apple-horseradish
steps.text: While the beef simmers, toss the grated apple with the lemon juice straight away, which stops it browning, then stir in the horseradish and sugar. Chill until needed.

steps.title: Make the chive sauce
steps.text: Stir the soured cream, chives, milk, salt and pepper together in a bowl, then chill alongside the apple-horseradish. The milk loosens the soured cream just enough to make a spoonable sauce rather than a thick dollop.

steps.title: Cook the potatoes
steps.text: About 25 minutes before the beef is ready, boil the potatoes in unsalted water until tender, then drain and toss with the butter and chives. Timing them to finish just as the beef is ready means everything reaches the table hot together.

steps.title: Rest and carve the beef
steps.text: Lift the beef out of the broth and rest it under foil for 10 minutes before carving. Resting lets the juices settle back through the meat after hours of gentle simmering, so it slices more cleanly.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Strain the broth and cut the carrots, parsnip and celeriac into bite-sized pieces. Slice the beef 1 cm thick against the grain, lay it in warmed shallow bowls with the vegetables, ladle over a little hot broth, and serve with the potatoes and both sauces.

tips: Skim the broth carefully during the first 10-15 minutes of simmering — missing this step is the main reason a broth turns cloudy instead of clear.
Keep the beef at a bare simmer for the full cooking time rather than a rolling boil; boiling toughens the meat instead of tenderising it.
Toss the grated apple with lemon juice the moment it's cut, or it will brown and look unappetising in the finished relish.
Check doneness with a skewer rather than a set time alone, since the exact simmering time can vary with the shape and thickness of the beef.
safety: Save any extra broth rather than discarding it — it makes a good base for a simple soup; just reheat it to 74°C before serving.
storage: Refrigerate leftover beef, vegetables and broth separately in covered containers for up to 3 days; the broth also freezes well for up to 3 months. Reheat the beef and broth together gently until piping hot throughout (74°C), and serve the sauces freshly stirred rather than reheated. Cool leftovers in a shallow container and refrigerate within 2 hours (within 1 hour on a day above 32°C).
